title: The Undertow of Room 214
premise: Gideon Brightwater, a translator who has spent thirty years cataloguing the words of her dying childhood language—and everything she never said in it—hears an unrecorded song on a late-night radio program, one written by her brother the summer before he drowned. The broadcast pulls her back to Salt Hollow, the fading coastal town where the story went wrong, now slated for demolition. As she pieces together who kept the song alive and why it surfaced now, Gideon must confront the night her silence cost her family everything, reconcile with the found family that formed in her absence, and choose whether to let Room 214—the boarding-house room where her brother's last words were spoken—fall with the building or carry its story forward. The novel ends at the demolition date: Gideon translates the song aloud in the old tongue for the gathered townsfolk, then lets the walls come down, keeping only what can be carried.
about_author: Cyrus Ravensworth is the pen name of a former court interpreter who spent a decade documenting endangered coastal dialects before turning to fiction. They write from a houseboat on the northern Atlantic, where they claim the tide dictates their deadlines.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Gideon, working late on a translation commission in her city apartment, catalogs borrowed words replacing her childhood tongue—her private ledger of loss. A phone call about her mother's estate goes unanswered. POV: Gideon. Emotional beat: quiet grief disguised as professional detachment; the reader feels a life organized around avoidance.

chapters.title: A Song That Was Never Recorded
chapters.summary: Driving home through rain, Gideon hears a folk program play a song she knows was never recorded—her brother Tam's composition from the last summer of his life. She nearly drives off the road. The host credits 'a listener in Salt Hollow.' POV: Gideon. Emotional beat: shock cracking open decades of sealed memory; the past becomes suddenly, terrifyingly present.

chapters.title: What the Radio Wouldn't Say
chapters.summary: Gideon tracks the station, learns the recording came from an anonymous cassette mailed to the show, postmarked Salt Hollow. Her editor notices her unraveling mid-deadline. She books a room at the Wrenfield boarding house without admitting to herself why. POV: Gideon. Emotional beat: compulsion overriding resistance; the first step of a return she swore never to make.

chapters.title: Salt Hollow, Half-Demolished
chapters.summary: Gideon arrives to find the town half-gutted, condemned buildings marked in orange paint, demolition set for six weeks out. The Wrenfield still stands. At the front desk she meets Odile Wrenfield, who recognizes her instantly and says nothing. POV: Gideon. Emotional beat: disorientation and dread; home rendered unrecognizable mirrors her own estrangement.

chapters.title: Room 214
chapters.summary: Odile assigns Gideon Room 214—the room where Tam spent his final summer and spoke his last words. Gideon demands another room; Odile refuses, gently. That night Gideon finds pencil lyrics ghosting the wallpaper beneath layers of paint. POV: Gideon. Emotional beat: claustrophobic confrontation with the exact site of trauma; no more distance possible.

chapters.title: The People Who Stayed
chapters.summary: In the Wrenfield's kitchen, Gideon meets the boarding house's ragged constellation of residents: Marisol, a retired fisherwoman; Dev, a teenage runaway Odile quietly shelters; and old Piotr, who claims he remembers Tam's voice. POV: alternating Gideon and Dev. Emotional beat: wary curiosity; the beginnings of a found family Gideon doesn't yet trust herself to join.

chapters.title: Who Sent the Cassette
chapters.summary: Gideon asks the radio host for the sender's name; the envelope bore no signature, only a line of the old language written phonetically—wrongly, by someone who learned it secondhand. Someone outside the family preserved what she abandoned. POV: Gideon. Emotional beat: shame sharpened into urgency; a stranger guarded her inheritance better than she did.

chapters.title: Marisol's Version
chapters.summary: Marisol reveals she heard Tam sing that song the week he died, down at the breakwater, and that Gideon's mother banned it from the house afterward. She hums a verse Gideon has never heard. POV: Marisol. Emotional beat: the town's collective memory contradicting Gideon's private one; grief revealed as something shared, not solely hers.

chapters.title: The Demolition Notice
chapters.summary: Official notice arrives: the Wrenfield is on the demolition list, date confirmed. Residents scatter to find housing; Dev panics—he has nowhere legal to go. Odile stays unnervingly calm. POV: Dev. Emotional beat: fear of losing belonging just as it forms; stakes become concrete and time-bound.

chapters.title: Phonetics of a Ghost
chapters.summary: Gideon deciphers the cassette liner's misspelled phrase: 'the tide keeps what we give it.' It's a line from Tam's notebook—which means someone read that notebook after his death. She begins searching the half-demolished house where they grew up. POV: Gideon. Emotional beat: detective-like momentum masking dread; every clue points toward the night she has never reconstructed.

chapters.title: Piotr Remembers Wrong
chapters.summary: Piotr tells a version of Tam's last night that contradicts the official drowning account: there were three people on the breakwater, not two. He names no one, but looks at Gideon when he says it. POV: Piotr. Emotional beat: vertigo; the reader and Gideon both begin suspecting her own buried memory holds the answer.

chapters.title: The Notebook in the Wall
chapters.summary: Gideon pries loose a board in the old house and finds Tam's notebook, water-warped but legible—full of songs, and a final entry addressed to her by name. She cannot bring herself to read past the first line. POV: Gideon. Emotional beat: terror of knowledge; the truth is literally in her hands and she flinches from it.

chapters.title: Dev's Night Out
chapters.summary: Dev, spooked by the demolition notice, runs—but returns soaked at 3 a.m., having stood on the same breakwater. Gideon sits with him without questions, sharing cocoa and silence. POV: Dev. Emotional beat: two runaways recognizing each other; the found family begins functioning as refuge rather than threat.

chapters.title: Odile's Ledger
chapters.summary: Odile shows Gideon the boarding house register: her mother stayed in Room 214 for a month, twenty years ago, the year before she died—and paid for the room with the very cassette later mailed to the radio station. POV: Odile. Emotional beat: revelation reframing everything; her mother carried the guilt too, and chose preservation over confession.

chapters.title: What Gideon Did Not Say
chapters.summary: Reading Tam's final entry at last, Gideon reconstructs the night: Tam asked her to run away with him; she refused and said nothing when he went to the breakwater alone in a storm—because she was angry. The third person Piotr saw was her mother, who arrived too late. POV: Gideon. Emotional beat: devastating self-confrontation; survival's price made explicit—she lived because she stayed silent.

chapters.title: The Argument in the Kitchen
chapters.summary: Gideon, raw, accuses Odile of engineering everything—the room, the cassette timeline—as penance-by-proxy. Odile answers that some debts are paid by keeping doors open, not by closing them. Dev overhears everything. POV: Gideon. Emotional beat: rupture within the fragile found family; Gideon weaponizes honesty to avoid receiving it.

chapters.title: Low Tide
chapters.summary: Alone at the breakwater at low tide, Gideon finds the physical evidence: Tam's harmonica wedged in the rocks, exactly where a body would have been pulled out. She sings the unfinished verse aloud in the old language, voice breaking. POV: Gideon. Emotional beat: catharsis at the site of loss; mourning finally performed instead of postponed.

chapters.title: The Verse Nobody Knew
chapters.summary: Back at the Wrenfield, Gideon completes the song using Tam's notebook and her own fluency—the last fluent speaker of the dialect. Marisol adds a harmony; Dev records it on his phone. For the first time, the song exists whole. POV: alternating Gideon and Marisol. Emotional beat: collaborative creation; grief transmuted into something shared and living.

chapters.title: Petition for the Wrenfield
chapters.summary: Galvanized, the residents fight the demolition: Marisol works her council connections, Dev documents the building's history, Gideon drafts the heritage appeal in language that moves even the clerk. They lose the appeal—but win a stay of one week and permission to hold a farewell gathering. POV: Dev. Emotional beat: defiant solidarity; losing gracefully while gaining each other.

chapters.title: The Last Night of Room 214
chapters.summary: On the eve of demolition, the boarding house fills with former residents and townsfolk. Gideon stands in Room 214, reads Tam's full entry aloud, then forgives herself—not absolution, but release. Odile gives her the original cassette. POV: Gideon. Emotional beat: tender culmination; the room emptied of its secret, filled instead with witnesses.

chapters.title: Demolition Day
chapters.summary: Before the excavators arrive, Gideon leads the assembled crowd in the completed song, sung in the old tongue—many voices carrying a language one throat could no longer hold alone. The Wrenfield comes down as they finish the final verse. POV: Gideon. Emotional beat: climax and exorcism; destruction and transmission happening in the same breath.

chapters.title: Undertow, Turning
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Gideon teaches a Saturday class in Salt Hollow's community center—Dev, Marisol, and a dozen others learning the old words. She begins a new inventory, this one of things said. The novel closes as she writes Tam's name at the top of the list, correctly spelled. POV: Gideon. Emotional beat: resolution; belonging chosen rather than inherited, survival redefined as carrying others forward.
